title: Lift up your gates (Psalm 23 [24])
hook: the earth is the Lord's, and the king of glory comes in

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shepherd, who leads through the valley, not around it. Your line was I shall want nothing. Today, a psalm with a procession in it.

A crowd climbs a hill toward a walled city, singing. At the front, carried on poles, is the ark, the gold-covered chest that, in Israel's scriptures, marks the presence of the invisible God. The city gates are shut. The crowd calls up to them, the watchmen on the walls call back a question, and the crowd answers. Call and response, like a stadium chant. Psalm 23 in the Douay, 24 in most Bibles, may well be the script for that moment.
screen: `A CROWD CLIMBING A HILL.` → `THE ARK AT THE FRONT.` → `THE GATES ARE SHUT.`

segments.voice: It opens wide: "The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof: the world, and all they that dwell therein." The ground, the sea, every person on it. Saint Paul quotes this line to settle an argument about food: eat what's sold in the market, he says, because the earth is the Lord's. Then the question at the foot of the hill: "Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord: or who shall stand in his holy place?" The answer isn't a bloodline or a title: "The innocent in hands, and clean of heart." Clean hands, meaning what you do. A clean heart, meaning what you want. Then the gates: "Lift up your gates, O ye princes, and be ye lifted up, O eternal gates: and the King of Glory shall enter in." From the wall, the challenge: "Who is this King of Glory?" And the crowd: the Lord who is strong and mighty. It happens twice, a chant that builds. Christian readers have heard Christ here: some heard his entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, some the Ascension, heaven's gates opening. An old Christian story tells of Christ going down to the dead on Holy Saturday, and the gates of the underworld hearing this very psalm before they break. And in the older Roman rite of Palm Sunday, the procession stopped outside the shut church door, someone knocked with the foot of the cross, and the gates were sung open.
screen: `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` · `CLEAN HANDS, CLEAN HEART.` · `WHO IS THIS KING OF GLORY?` · `THE DOOR KNOCKED WITH A CROSS.`

segments.voice: Open a window or a door slowly, on purpose, and stand there breathing the outside air; if you can't reach one, picture a door in your home opening wide. Think of the psalm's first line: the street, the neighbors, the weather, all of it the Lord's. If you pray, say lift up your gates, and let God in; if you don't, let the open door be a way of welcoming the day.
Attollite portas. Latin for lift up your gates, the psalm's cry at the city wall, so the King of Glory can come in. Today's word.
Your line: the earth is the lord's. Every bit of it, even the ordinary streets. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 23 [24] in the Liturgy of the Hours, sometimes as the opening Invitatory psalm, and hear it at Mass in Advent and on feasts like the Presentation of the Lord.

notes: Douay Psalm 23 wording: confirm against a Challoner edition.
The ark procession setting is a common scholarly reconstruction (cf. 2 Samuel 6), hedged 'may well be'.
Harrowing of hell: the Gospel of Nicodemus (Descent into Hell) uses Psalm 24's gate dialogue; described as 'an old Christian story', not scripture. Confirm.
Palm Sunday rite before 1955: the subdeacon knocked on the closed church door with the processional cross while the Gloria, laus was sung (the dialogue drew on Attollite portas). Confirm details.
